entries.answer:
Exa’s full platform is a layered system: it continuously turns the changing public web into clean, structured, embedded documents; serves those documents through fast multi-index retrieval and reranking; then exposes the resulting capabilities as APIs for search, content extraction, agentic research, structured outputs, and continuously updated entity datasets.

The shortest architecture diagram is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Web}
\rightarrow
\text{crawl + parse}
\rightarrow
\text{store + derive signals}
\rightarrow
\text{embed + index}
\rightarrow
\text{retrieve + fuse + rerank}
\rightarrow
\text{extract relevant evidence}
\rightarrow
\text{search / agents / Websets / API products}
}
\]

## 1. Web ingestion

Exa begins with a continuous crawl-and-refresh operation—not a finished one-time “download of the web.”

\[
\text{URL discovery}
\rightarrow
\text{fetch}
\rightarrow
\text{parse}
\rightarrow
\text{detect changes}
\rightarrow
\text{reprocess changed pages}
\]

The crawler discovers and revisits URLs, fetches pages across a distributed fleet, parses HTML and other formats, and maintains a high-quality searchable subset of the web. The system must handle HTML, PDFs, JavaScript-rendered apps, multimedia, variable update rates, duplicates, redirects, dead URLs, and pages that change from hourly news updates to effectively immutable academic papers.[1][2]

A useful mental model is that the crawler produces a raw web-record layer:

```text
URL
canonical URL
HTTP and crawl status
fetch timestamp
raw response/content
content type
redirect history
outgoing links
change fingerprint
```

That data is not yet a useful search index. It is the raw material for parsing and model-generated signals.

## 2. Parse and derive data

Each fetched document becomes many derived artifacts:

\[
\text{raw page}
\rightarrow
\{
\text{clean main text},
\text{title and metadata},
\text{language},
\text{page chunks},
\text{links},
\text{content type},
\text{quality signals},
\text{embeddings},
\text{structured extractions}
\}
\]

The parser removes or de-emphasizes boilerplate such as navigation, consent banners, repeated footers, ads, sidebars, and template content. It identifies the actual article, documentation section, research paper, repository description, company page, or profile content that should influence search.

Exa’s in-house **exa-d** framework represents those artifacts as typed data columns with declared dependencies:

\[
\text{raw document}
\rightarrow
\text{parsed text}
\rightarrow
\text{tokens}
\rightarrow
\text{embedding}
\rightarrow
\text{index representation}
\]

It stores web data in Lance datasets on S3. Lance fragments can have partial schemas, allowing Exa to write or replace a single derived column—such as `embedding_v2`—for a particular fragment without rewriting every field for every page.[2]

## 3. Incremental index pipeline

The central challenge is avoiding a full rebuild every time a page changes or Exa deploys a new model.

Exa computes the difference between:

\[
\text{desired state}
\]

and:

\[
\text{currently materialized state}
\]

Then it computes only missing or invalid data:

\[
\text{required work}
=
\text{desired derived columns}
-
\text{valid stored derived columns}
\]

For example:

| Event | Recomputed work |
|---|---|
| New URL is crawled | Parse, metadata, chunks, embeddings, index insertion |
| Existing page text changes | Reparse, refresh dependent embeddings/signals, update index |
| New embedding model version | Re-embed stored parsed documents; no network recrawl required |
| Parser bug affects some fragments | Invalidate/recompute only the affected fields/fragments |
| A new search signal is added | Backfill only that added derived column |

`exa-d` topologically sorts dependency graphs, runs only unfinished work, checkpoints progress at fragment level, and resumes after partial failures.[2]

### Distributed compute

The physical execution layer uses Ray Data and Ray Actors:

\[
\text{S3/network input}
\parallel
\text{CPU parsing/tokenization}
\parallel
\text{GPU embedding inference}
\parallel
\text{storage/index writes}
\]

Ray Actors keep expensive models loaded in GPU memory across batches. This avoids loading an embedding model repeatedly for every fragment and enables pipeline parallelism: while one fragment is embedded on a GPU, another can be tokenized and another fetched from S3.[2]

## 4. Neural document index

After parsing, Exa’s custom transformer embedding models turn documents or document chunks into vectors:

\[
\text{document/chunk}
\rightarrow
E_d(\text{document})
\rightarrow
\mathbf{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{4096}
\]

At query time:

\[
\text{user query}
\rightarrow
E_q(\text{query})
\rightarrow
\mathbf{q}
\]

The model is trained so that documents matching the query’s intent occupy nearby regions of embedding space. This supports semantic retrieval: a request can find relevant sources even where they use different words from the user’s phrasing.

Exa’s intended distinction is:

\[
\text{keyword overlap}
\neq
\text{actual relevance}
\]

For example, a request for “open-source Python libraries for constrained Bayesian optimization” should retrieve an actual repository or documentation page above a generic article that repeats the phrase many times.

## 5. Custom vector database

The web-scale vector store is the fast retrieval engine. Exa says it can search billions of vectors in under 100 ms while supporting keyword and metadata filters.[3]

Its published first-stage retrieval design is:

\[
\text{4,096-d embedding}
\rightarrow
\text{256-d Matryoshka prefix}
\rightarrow
\text{1-bit binary document vector}
\rightarrow
\text{cluster assignment}
\]

### Matryoshka embeddings

Exa trains embeddings so early vector dimensions still preserve usable semantic meaning:

\[
\mathbf{e}_{4096}
\supset
\mathbf{e}_{2048}
\supset
\mathbf{e}_{1024}
\supset
\mathbf{e}_{256}
\]

It stores the first 256 dimensions for the fast path, which it says reduces memory by 20×.[3]

### Binary quantization

Each 16-bit document-vector coordinate becomes a one-bit sign:

\[
d_i
\mapsto
\begin{cases}
+1 & d_i > 0\\
-1 & d_i \le 0
\end{cases}
\]

A 256-dimensional document vector then occupies:

\[
256 \text{ bits} = 32 \text{ bytes}
\]

rather than 512 bytes at 16-bit precision. Exa reports another 16× memory reduction.[3]

### Float-query × binary-document scoring

The query stays in floating point, while documents stay binary:

\[
s(q,d)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{256}q_i b_i
\]

This preserves which query features matter strongly while keeping stored document vectors compact.

Exa speeds this score using lookup tables for small binary subvectors, keeps tables in CPU registers, and says the most performance-critical kernel was implemented in **C++ rather than Rust**.[3]

### Cluster routing

Documents are split into roughly 100,000 semantic clusters:

\[
\text{query embedding}
\rightarrow
\text{nearest cluster(s)}
\rightarrow
\text{search only local candidates}
\]

The system searches the cluster where the query lands plus nearby clusters rather than comparing against the entire corpus. Exa reports roughly a 1,000× throughput improvement from this clustering approach with little accuracy degradation.[3]

### Filter indexes

Alongside the vector structure, Exa maintains inverted indexes for filterable values:

\[
\text{domain/date/category/keyword}
\rightarrow
\text{matching document IDs}
\]

A filtered request becomes:

\[
\text{semantic cluster candidates}
\cap
\text{filter-eligible document IDs}
\]

So a request constrained to a date range, specific domain, category, or keyword does not retrieve globally and throw almost everything away afterward.[3]

## 6. Multi-stage ranking

The compressed vector index is intended for **high recall**, not final ordering.

\[
\text{query}
\rightarrow
\text{fast approximate retrieval}
\rightarrow
\text{top-}K\text{ candidates}
\rightarrow
\text{full/uncompressed reranking}
\rightarrow
\text{final results}
\]

The first stage is lossy:

- 4,096 dimensions are reduced to 256.
- Document values are reduced to one bit.
- Only nearby clusters are searched.

Exa repairs the resulting ranking loss by retrieving extra candidates and reranking them with uncompressed information.[3]

A conceptual final score can combine several signals:

\[
S(q,d)
=
S_{\text{dense}}
+
S_{\text{sparse}}
+
S_{\text{reranker}}
+
S_{\text{freshness}}
+
S_{\text{metadata}}
\]

The precise model architecture and weights are proprietary, but Exa publicly confirms custom embedding models and custom reranking models.[4][3]

## 7. Multi-index search fusion

Exa does not rely on a single index for every query. A query can use several candidate generators:

\[
\begin{cases}
\text{dense neural web index}\\
\text{sparse inverted/keyword index}\\
\text{publication index}\\
\text{people/company indexes}\\
\text{fresh/news-oriented path}\\
\text{knowledge or product graph}
\end{cases}
\]

For dense-plus-sparse search, Exa publicly shows **reciprocal rank fusion**:

\[
\operatorname{RRF}(d)
=
\sum_{r}
\frac{1}{k+\operatorname{rank}_r(d)}
\]

The result lists are fused before content fetch and later reranking.[5]

For publication search, Exa says it searches both the general web index and a dedicated publications index, then combines and reranks results.[6]

## 8. Canon orchestration

The online search path is coordinated by **Canon**, Exa’s in-house search-pipeline orchestrator.

Canon represents a request as a typed DAG:

\[
\text{classify}
\rightarrow
\begin{cases}
\text{dense retrieval}\\
\text{sparse retrieval}\\
\text{specialized retrieval}
\end{cases}
\rightarrow
\text{fuse}
\rightarrow
\text{fetch}
\rightarrow
\text{rerank}
\rightarrow
\text{serve}
\]

Canon’s runtime provides:

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| Parallel scheduling | Runs independent retrieval/ranking branches together |
| Pull-based evaluation | Runs upstream work only when a downstream result needs it |
| Request-local memoization | Computes a shared node once even if several branches need it |
| Cancellation propagation | Stops work after timeouts, client disconnects, or lost races |
| Local retries | Retries a failed node without rerunning successful ancestors |
| Typed graph validation | Makes dependencies and outcome handling explicit |
| Full tracing | Records inputs, outputs, timing, cancellation, and failures |

Exa designed Canon for online search paths that may need classification, localization, retrieval, filters, ranking, and multiple indexes within a roughly 250 ms serving budget.[5]

## 9. Query-specific content extraction

Finding the correct page is not always enough. A page can contain tens of thousands of tokens while the answer is a single paragraph.

Exa’s **Highlights** system extracts dense, query-specific passages:

\[
\text{query + candidate page}
\rightarrow
\text{chunk/embed/score}
\rightarrow
\text{best evidence excerpts}
\]

Exa says highlights run on every request, are not cached because relevance depends on the query, and complete in under 100 ms. They are designed to provide the relevant evidence with much less context than entire pages.[7]

For agentic workflows, this changes the data path:

\[
\text{search results}
\rightarrow
\text{query-relevant highlights}
\rightarrow
\text{agent reasoning}
\]

rather than:

\[
\text{search results}
\rightarrow
\text{full raw web pages}
\rightarrow
\text{large, noisy agent context}
\]

Exa says its `/answer`, Deep, and Websets agentic endpoints use highlights as the retrieval substrate on every agent-loop iteration rather than reading raw page content by default.[7]

## 10. User-facing platform

Everything above becomes several developer and user products.

| Platform layer | What it provides |
|---|---|
| Search API | Semantic web search with modes, categories, filters, and ranked results |
| Contents API | Clean extracted page content, highlights, summaries, and related output controls |
| Answer API | Search-backed answer generation |
| Context / Exa Code | Fast coding-oriented retrieval over code/web sources |
| Deep / Deep Reasoning | Agentic multi-step search, query expansion, synthesis, structured output, and grounding |
| Agent API | Long-running research runs and multi-turn continuation |
| Websets | Persistent entity discovery, verification, enrichment, and monitoring |
| Monitors | Scheduled repeated searches and update delivery |
| SDKs / MCP / integrations | Client-side access from Python, TypeScript, agent frameworks, and coding environments |

Exa’s API platform publicly lists Search, Contents, Answer, Context, Agent API, Monitors, Websets, and SDKs as the main surfaces built on top of its search infrastructure.[8]

## 11. Agentic product path

For a complex question, Exa Deep adds an agentic layer over normal retrieval:

\[
\text{user request}
\rightarrow
\text{intent analysis}
\rightarrow
\text{parallel subqueries}
\rightarrow
\text{Exa search}
\rightarrow
\text{highlights/evidence}
\rightarrow
\text{LLM reasoning}
\rightarrow
\text{synthesis}
\rightarrow
\text{grounded output}
\]

Exa says Deep uses query expansion, LLM reasoning, multiple search agents in parallel, and result synthesis. It offers `deep` and `deep-reasoning` modes; its published latency ranges are 4–12 seconds for `deep` and 12–50 seconds for `deep-reasoning`.[9]

For long-running entity collection, Websets adds a durable asynchronous loop:

\[
\text{create entity search}
\rightarrow
\text{discover candidates}
\rightarrow
\text{verify criteria}
\rightarrow
\text{enrich accepted items}
\rightarrow
\text{emit updates}
\rightarrow
\text{monitor for future changes}
\]

## Full end-to-end example

Imagine a user asks:

> “Find recent open-source Python libraries for constrained Bayesian optimization, prioritize official documentation and maintained repositories.”

The platform path looks like:

```text
1. User/API request arrives
   └─ Query type: technical/software discovery
   └─ Optional constraints: recent, open source, Python, constrained BO

2. Canon selects a search graph
   └─ Dense semantic retrieval
   └─ Sparse exact-term/code retrieval
   └─ Optional code-specific or documentation path
   └─ Date/domain/category filters

3. Retrieval
   └─ Query becomes a float embedding
   └─ Nearest semantic clusters are selected
   └─ Binary-quantized document vectors are scanned
   └─ Filter inverted indexes restrict eligible documents
   └─ Sparse and dense candidate lists are created

4. Fusion and ranking
   └─ Candidate lists are combined, e.g. RRF
   └─ Extra candidates are fetched
   └─ Full-precision/richer reranking promotes direct repositories and docs

5. Evidence extraction
   └─ Highlights locate relevant constraint-support, install, API, license,
      repository, and maintenance passages

6. Product response
   └─ Search API: ranked URLs + summaries/highlights/content
   └─ Deep: multi-source answer with citations or structured fields
   └─ Websets: persistent verified list of matching libraries
```

```text

exa-d dependency graph
```

The main insight is that Exa is not merely “an embedding model plus a vector database.” It is an integrated web-data system:

\[
\boxed{
\text{continuous crawl}
+
\text{incremental data engineering}
+
\text{custom semantic models}
+
\text{compressed web-scale vector retrieval}
+
\text{multi-index fusion}
+
\text{neural reranking}
+
\text{query-specific evidence extraction}
+
\text{agentic APIs}
}
\]

That is the path from an unstructured, changing public web page to a fast, user-usable search result, grounded answer, structured research output, or continuously maintained Webset.
